# Remanufactured 5.3 Engine Not Firing on One Bank

Installing a remanufactured engine often feels like hitting the reset button, but electrical and mechanical mismatches between donor components can still leave you with a half-functional vehicle. In your case, a 2007 Chevy Avalanche 5.3L V8 running only Bank 1 (cylinders 1, 3, 5, 7) while Bank 2 (2, 4, 6, 8) receives no spark indicates an upstream failure specific to that bank's ignition or sensor circuit. Since you have already replaced the camshaft position sensor, crankshaft position sensor, and all four oxygen sensors without resolving the issue, we need to shift our diagnostic focus from primary timing signals to secondary ignition delivery and compression integrity.

The fact that the engine runs on Bank 1 suggests the PCM (Powertrain Control Module) is receiving valid RPM and timing data from the common sensors shared by both banks. On the GM 5.3L Vortec Gen III/IV architecture, the primary spark is generated by the coil-on-plug (COP) system. Each cylinder has its own ignition coil mounted directly atop the spark plug. If Bank 2 cylinders are not firing despite having power at the coil pack connectors, the fault usually lies within one of three areas: a failed internal coil, a broken ground path for the coils, or a lack of primary control signal from the PCM.

Verify the power and ground integrity on Bank 2 before condemning the entire engine block. Use a multimeter to check for 12 volts at the main power feed wire (usually yellow/red) and continuity on the ground straps connecting the coil pack housing to the engine block. A common pitfall with remanufactured engines is that while the internal components are new, the external harness or mounting points may be corroded or improperly torqued during installation. If the coils cannot complete a circuit to ground, they will not fire even if the PCM sends a pulse.

Next, inspect the primary control side of the ignition system. The PCM controls the spark by switching the ground path for each coil individually. You can isolate whether the issue is the PCM output or the internal coil by performing a swap test. Remove one working coil from Bank 1 and install it in Bank 2 at cylinder 8 (or any position on that bank). Start the engine:
- If the new spark appears on Bank 2, the original coils were internally shorted or defective. This is a frequent issue with remanufactured units where internal windings fail after installation due to voltage spikes.
- If Bank 2 still remains dead while using a known good coil from Bank 1, the problem is likely the PCM driver circuit for that specific bank or a wiring harness break between the PCM and the coil pack connectors.

Check the secondary ignition components as well. While less common than primary failures, inspect the spark plugs on Bank 2. If the engine was run briefly in this state, carbon buildup could prevent combustion even if spark is present. However, your description of "no spark" points more strongly to electrical delivery. Ensure that you are testing for spark correctly; using a timing light or a dedicated spark tester is safer than relying solely on visual inspection, as modern coils can produce high voltage without an actual ground path through the plug.

If all wiring, grounds, and swapped coils confirm no signal from the PCM side of the connector, and the harness is intact, the PCM itself may have failed to output control signals for Bank 2. This is rare but possible if there was a voltage spike during installation that damaged the driver transistors inside the module. In such cases, flash updates or reprogramming are sometimes attempted, but hardware replacement of the PCM is often required if internal drivers are blown.

Always cross-reference the VIN and engine code with the build sheet when installing remanufactured units to ensure the ECU calibration matches the vehicle's configuration. Mismatched calibrations can cause the PCM to enter a fail-safe mode that disables specific cylinders to prevent catalytic converter damage, though this usually triggers a Check Engine Light immediately rather than allowing partial operation without fault codes in some cases.

For deeper dives into GM 5.3L diagnostic procedures and wiring schematics, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can provide structured technical data if you need to map out the specific pinouts for your harness setup.
